newtons-second-law-def.title: Newton's Second Law
newtons-second-law-def.interpretation: The fundamental equation of Newtonian dynamics defines force as the time-rate of change of linear momentum. In an inertial frame, the net force acting on a system is equal to the momentum flux, characterizing force as the generator of translational state-changes in the 4D manifold.
newtons-second-law-def.symmetry_origin: The law is a specific manifestation of the Galilean Group symmetry, ensuring that physical interactions remain invariant under shifts in inertial frames. In the analytical formalism, it is derived from the Principle of Least Action, where the extremization of the Lagrangian functional leads to the Euler-Lagrange equations of motion.
newtons-second-law-def.limits_and_boundary: In the classical limit (\( v \ll c \)), the law reduces to the constant-mass form \( \mathbf{F} = m\mathbf{a} \). It fails in the relativistic regime, where it must be replaced by the Minkowski 4-force \( K^\mu \), and in the quantum regime, where it emerges as an effective ontology for expectation values via Ehrenfest's Theorem.

noether-angular-momentum-charge-a4c362c8.symmetry_origin: The stationarity of the action functional under the continuous group SO(3).
noether-angular-momentum-charge-a4c362c8.limits_and_boundary: Remains a strict constant of motion ($d\mathbf{L}/dt = 0$) for any system in a central potential field.
